newsitem.title: INDIA: India's DoT to seek review of telecoms ruling.
newsitem.headline: India's DoT to seek review of telecoms ruling.

text.p: The state-run Department of Telecommunications (DoT) has decided to ask India's independent telecommunications regulator to review a ruling on call tariffs, a senior government official said on Monday.

But DoT had decided not to appeal against the ruling on calls made from fixed to mobile telephones in order to send the right signals to boost foreign investment, A.V.Gokak, chairman of the Telecom Commission, told a news conference.

"DoT has decided not to appeal against the decision, as this might have implications across the board. The psychology of the foreign investor is important to us, and we want to be seen as conducive to foreign investment," Gokak said.

Besides heading the commission, Gokak is also the most senior civil servant in the DoT, which has enjoyed a decades-old monopoly in telephone services. India ended the monopoly under an economic reforms programme launched in 1991.

The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India's (TRAI) order on April 25 rolled back fixed to mobile call tariffs to the earlier level of Rs 0.47 per minute, after DoT raised it to Rs 10 per minute from February 15.
DoT had issued its order on January 29 prompting private mobile phone firms to approach the TRAI set up in March to oversee the industry.
DoT was working out the financial implications of TRAI's decision and once the details are ready, it would seek a comprehensive review of the ruling, Gokak said.

"We are in genuine doubt about what the tariff should be for fixed to mobile calls, as none has been notified as yet. There are also issues concerning interconnectivity that have not been fully looked into," Gokak added.
DoT will commission a nationwide survey of subscribers to overcome a lack of data on telephone usage to compute the loss that would arise from rolling back the tariff hike, Gokak said.
He mentioned a government-funded agency, the National Council for Applied Economic Research (NCAER), as a likely choice to carry out the survey.
Long distance and international call rates in India, among the highest in the world, subsidise local calls, which are amongst the cheapest.
"These anomalies need to be rectified. We want to know what the scope for reducing these tariffs is," said Gokak.
